content.title: About
content.content: Fried calamari are rings or strips of squid meat that are deep‑fried in vegetable oil until golden and crisp. They have a tender, slightly sweet sea flavor and a crunchy texture. Commonly served as an appetizer in bars and restaurants, they also appear in salads, pastas, and Asian‑style dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Calamari belong to the cephalopod mollusks and are close relatives of octopuses and cuttlefish.
Squid flesh is very low in fat, but during frying it quickly absorbs oil, creating a crisp coating.
In Japan fried calamari are often served with soy sauce, lemon, and grated wasabi.
Calamari can change skin colour thanks to pigments, but after cooking they usually turn white or light pink.
In several countries fried calamari are a popular street‑food snack.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Calamari provide a complete marine protein that supports muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Raw squid contains about 92 kcal per 100 g, making it a diet‑friendly option when fried in moderation.

items.title: B‑vitamin source
items.content: They contain vitamin B12, niacin and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Calamari supply zinc, selenium and iodine, nutrients that support immunity and thyroid function.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Although in smaller amounts than fatty fish, calamari still provide EPA and DHA.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to squid, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Heavy‑metal content
items.content: Squid can accumulate cadmium and mercury; moderate consumption is advised, especially for pregnant women and children.

items.title: High sodium when seasoned
items.content: Adding salt or sauces during frying can raise sodium levels, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked squid may harbor bacteria or parasites; ensure thorough cooking to safe internal temperature.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve fried calamari hot, sprinkled with salt, lemon juice, or spices. They can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, tossed into salads, rice or noodle dishes, and used in tacos or sushi rolls.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fried calamari in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a zip‑lock bag at –18 °C; reheat in the oven or skillet before serving to restore crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Lo Mein is a classic Chinese stir‑fried noodle dish made from wheat flour noodles. The NFS (3559) version is a ready‑to‑cook kit that includes noodles, sauce, vegetables, and spices, allowing you to prepare an authentic meal at home quickly.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Lo Mein originated in Jiangsu province in the early 20th century.
The name literally means “tossed noodles.”
Traditional recipes use soy sauce, sesame oil, and ginger for flavor.
It is often served with a fried egg, beef, or shrimp.
In Japan a similar concept exists as ramen, but with different seasoning.

items.title: Carbohydrate source
items.content: The noodles provide a quick source of energy for active lifestyles.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains B1, B2 and B6 vitamins that support metabolism.

items.title: Contains vegetables
items.content: The vegetable mix (carrot, cabbage, onion) adds fiber and antioxidants.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Prepared without heavy frying, the dish remains relatively light.

items.title: Protein boost with meat additions
items.content: Adding beef, chicken or tofu increases complete protein content.

items.title: Gluten content
items.content: Wheat‑based noodles are unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sodium in sauce
items.content: Soy sauce can be high in salt; those with hypertension should limit usage.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: The sauce may trigger reactions in individuals allergic to soy.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Noodles can raise blood sugar quickly, so diabetics should consume in moderation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook the noodles according to the package (usually 3‑5 minutes), drain. In a pan heat a little oil, stir‑fry the vegetables, add noodles, sauce and spices, toss for 2‑3 minutes. Optionally add meat, tofu or a fried egg.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry ingredients in a sealed container in a cool, dry place. Cooked Lo Mein is best eaten within 1‑2 days and should be refrigerated.

content.title: About
content.content: The Peanut Butter and Jelly (PB&J) sandwich is a classic quick snack made of two slices of bread spread with peanut butter and fruit jelly. It combines protein, healthy fats, and carbohydrates, providing energy and satiety.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: PB&J has become an icon of American culture, appearing in movies, songs, and advertising.
The first commercial PB&J recipe appeared in the early 1900s when canned jelly and peanut butter entered the market.
The sandwich is convenient to take on the go, often used in school lunches and camping trips.
There are many variations: different fruit spreads, nut butters, or added banana slices are common.
In the 2020s, U.S. peanut butter sales grew over 10% driven by the popularity of PB&J.

items.title: Rich in protein and healthy fats
items.content: Peanut butter provides plant protein and monounsaturated fats that support heart health.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Both peanut butter and whole‑grain bread contain thiamine, niacin, and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants from the jelly
items.content: Fruit jelly supplies vitamin C and polyphenols that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Quick energy boost
items.content: Carbohydrates from the bread and sugars in the jelly rapidly replenish blood glucose.

items.title: Supports gut microbiota
items.content: Whole‑grain bread provides prebiotic fiber that feeds beneficial intestinal bacteria.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanut butter can trigger severe allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Store‑bought jelly often contains added sugar, which can contribute to weight gain and blood‑sugar spikes.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A PB&J sandwich is relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Some peanut butter varieties are salted; those monitoring sodium should choose unsalted versions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Spread an even layer of peanut butter on one slice of bread, add a layer of jelly on top, and place the second slice over it. The sandwich can be cut in half, toasted, or enhanced with banana, honey, or nuts for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep a prepared sandwich in an airtight container at room temperature for no more than 4 hours. Store opened peanut butter and jelly in the refrigerator, and keep bread in a dry place or sealed bag.

content.title: About
content.content: Pineapple salad with dressing is a refreshing mix of fresh vegetables, pineapple chunks, and a light aromatic dressing made from olive oil, lemon juice, and a touch of honey. It’s perfect as a light dish in warm weather or as a side to main courses.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pineapple contains bromelain – an enzyme that aids protein digestion.
The sweet‑sour balance of pineapple and dressing is a classic combination in Asian cuisine.
The salad can be prepared quickly: just chop the ingredients and toss with the dressing.
Pineapple is rich in vitamin C, which boosts immunity and supports skin health.
For vegetarians and vegans the salad is fully suitable if a honey‑free sweetener is used.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system, aids collagen synthesis, and improves iron absorption.

items.title: Contains bromelain
items.content: Bromelain helps digestion, reduces inflammation, and may aid muscle recovery after exercise.

items.title: Low‑calorie
items.content: The salad is low in calories yet provides a feeling of fullness thanks to vegetable fiber.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy gut function, regulates blood sugar, and contributes to lasting satiety.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: Olive oil in the dressing supplies monounsaturated fats that are heart‑friendly.

items.title: Pineapple allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pineapple, such as itching, swelling, or hives.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The acidic dressing can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers, so moderate consumption is advised.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sweet pineapple raises blood sugar levels, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled, right after tossing, to keep the vegetables crisp and the pineapple fragrant. It can be paired with grilled chicken, tofu, or seafood for a more substantial meal.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Before serving, give it a quick stir to redistribute the dressing.

shrimp-and-noodles-with-soy-based-sauce.title: Shrimp and Noodles with Soy‑Based Sauce

content.title: About
content.content: The dish “Shrimp and Noodles with Soy‑Based Sauce” combines succulent seafood, delicate egg noodles, and a savory soy sauce. The shrimp cook quickly, while the sauce adds a rich umami flavor with a hint of sweetness and mild heat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The soy sauce used is traditionally fermented from soybeans, wheat, salt, and water.
Shrimp are one of the most widely consumed seafoods worldwide and are rich in protein and trace minerals.
Egg noodles, a staple in Asian cuisine, are made from wheat flour, eggs, and sometimes starch, giving them a firm yet tender bite.
Stir‑frying on high heat preserves the crisp texture of both shrimp and noodles.
The dish is often finished with scallions, toasted sesame seeds, or fresh cilantro for extra aroma.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Shrimp provide easily digestible marine protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with many meat dishes, shrimp are low in saturated fats, making them suitable for heart‑healthy diets.

items.title: Rich in iodine and selenium
items.content: These trace elements support thyroid function and act as antioxidants.

items.title: Carbohydrate energy from noodles
items.content: Egg noodles supply quick‑release glucose, fueling physical activity.

items.title: Fermented soy sauce offers probiotics
items.content: The fermentation process creates beneficial bacteria that may aid gut health.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience severe allergic reactions to shrimp.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Soy sauce is salty; people with hypertension should limit its use.

items.title: Possible contaminants
items.content: Shrimp can contain trace amounts of heavy metals or microplastics, so choose reputable sources.

items.title: Added monosodium glutamate
items.content: Certain soy sauces contain MSG, which can cause sensitivity in some people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot, straight from the wok. Garnish with sliced scallions, toasted sesame seeds, or fresh cilantro. A squeeze of lime or a dash of chili sauce can add extra brightness if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. Shrimp and noodles are not ideal for freezing, as they may lose their texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit waffles are a ready‑to‑eat frozen dessert consisting of crisp waffle layers filled with berry or fruit puree. The product is made from wheat flour, sugar, vegetable fats and natural fruit ingredients, then quickly frozen to preserve aroma and texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Waffles first appeared in Europe in the 17th century as a way to use leftover batter.
Fruit fillings are often made from berries harvested in season and then frozen to retain vitamins.
Freezing allows the product to be stored for up to 12 months without flavor loss.
Fruit waffles are popular as a quick breakfast or snack in schools and offices.
IQF (Individually Quick Frozen) technology keeps pieces separate, preventing them from sticking together.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Waffles provide fast‑digesting carbs that give an immediate energy boost.

items.title: Vitamins and antioxidants
items.content: The fruit layer is rich in vitamin C and other antioxidants that support the immune system.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with many traditional desserts, these waffles usually contain less saturated fat.

items.title: Convenient and portable
items.content: They can be quickly heated in a microwave or toaster, making them practical for busy lifestyles.

items.title: Calcium and iron
items.content: Some recipes use fortified flour, increasing calcium and iron content.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Waffles are typically made with wheat flour, so they are not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Fruit fillings may contain added sugar, which should be considered by individuals with diabetes or low‑sugar diets.

items.title: Over‑cooling
items.content: Improper reheating can make waffles too hard or overly soggy.

items.title: Freezer quality control
items.content: If stored above –18 °C, ice crystals can form, leading to texture and flavor degradation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the frozen waffles in a microwave (30‑60 seconds) or toast them until golden. Serve with yogurt, honey, nuts or fresh berries for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the waffles in a sealed package at –18 °C or lower. After opening, use within 3‑4 weeks. Do not thaw and refreeze the product.
